Music Chopin’s Ballades: Four Musical Stories How the Polish maestro revolutionized the piano by fusing classical rigor with romantic drama. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Chopin concert, 1887, by Henryk Siemiradzki. Chopin dedicated himself almost exclusively to the piano and is said to have revolutionized piano music. Public Domain Kenneth LaFave 7/18/2026 | Updated: 7/20/2026 0:00 X 1 Frederic Chopin (1810–1849) composed almost exclusively for the piano. Every work written by this Polish-born son of a French father and Polish mother featured the piano in some way. It was presented most often as a solo instrument but also as an accompaniment for cello and voice. Chopin assisted, more than any other single composer apart from Beethoven, in the piano’s transformation from parlor companion to powerful venue fo r romantic expression. Nowhere is this more evident than in his four ballades for piano. Exile and the Parisian Years Chopin's four piano ballades are seen as masterpieces of the Romantic era. Many think they were inspired by the poetry of Adam Mickiewicz, who dedicated his life to the struggle for Polish independence. Public Domain Chopin was raised in a cultured family outside Warsaw, showed great early talent, and attende d the W arsaw Conservatory in his teens. Following Poland’s failed rebellion in 1830, w hen imperial Ru ssia reasserted its rule, Chopin, wh ose sympathies lay wit h the rebels, fled to Paris, never to return to his beloved homeland. The composer’s brief adulthood there was spent primarily teaching rich students. Chopin’s output before 1835 was divided between large-scale works in traditional, classical forms—like sonatas and rondos—and smaller genre pieces, such as mazurkas and waltzes, where he flexed his melodic instincts. Starting in 1835 with the first of his four “ballades,” Chopin combined the structural complexity of those larger classical forms with the expressive, free gestures of his shorter works. In these extended musical essays, melodic freedom is wedded to formal integrity. Chopin’s piano ballades combined classical forms with expressive, Romantic-era styles. Public Domain James Huneker’s flagship Chopin biography reports that Chopin, upon presenting fellow composer Robert Schumann with a copy o f the first ballade in G minor, confessed he had bee n enticed to create the ballades by the poetry of fellow Polish patriot Adam Mickiewicz. Mickiewicz’ s poems were dramatic narratives aimed against Russian occupation. As solo piano works, Chopin’s ballad es lack words, yet in them one hears stories of struggle and courage that reflect Mickiewicz’s poems. Schumann’s famous remark about Chopin’s music seems especially apt as regards the ball ades: “The works of Chopin are cannons concealed amidst flowers.” The very name attached to all four sco res—ballad e—sends a distinct signal that here are stories told in music. Chopin was the first composer to use that word to label an instrumental work. Before that, “ballade” referred to a Renaissance vocal composition. Related Stories Tune in Today: Chopin’s ‘Raindrop’ and Teardrops Book Review: ‘Chopin’s Piano: In Search of the Instrument That Transformed Music’ In starkest outline, sonata form presents contrasting musical ideas that are developed and transformed. From the form’s beginnings onward, this transformation was a synthesis of the previous elements. Scholar Jim Samson notes that in t he ball ades, Chopin repurposes sonata form to result in “apotheosis rather than synthesis.” Drama has replaced dialogue. Inside the Scores: Four Paths of Musical Drama Here is the great Sviatoslav Richter playing all four ballades: ( Listen ) Ballade No. 1 in G Minor, Op. 23 (1835—36) is marked by extremes of tempo, dynamics, and texture. After a brief, slow introduction, the first subject is introduced (0:33), a searching melody marked mo derato. This grows into a waltz-like transition (1:28) that swirls toward hints of virtuoso fireworks until a second, distinctive subject is introduced, pianissimo (2:08), becoming faster and faster until it bursts into a heroic, hymn-like third and final subject (3:02). Closing materials bring the exposition to an end but without a full stop. At 4:10, the development starts with a memory of the first subject. Shortly, the heroic third subject reinserts itself, now fortissimo and in strident octaves (4:41). This sets off an extended virtuoso climax that results in a sardonic paraphrase of the second subject (5:28). We hear the third subject one last time, quietly at first, then rising in waves. At 6:41 begins a foreshortened recapitulation. The first subject is dutifully repea ted, then su cceeded by a coda of fiery virtuosic scales and octaves, bringing t he first ballade to a shockingly dramatic conclusion. Each remain ing ballad e is distinctly different from the first and from one another. Here’s a general guide: Ballade No. 2, O p. 38 (1839), begins in a barcarolle rhythm that gently rocks a lyrical theme in F major. But the key of A minor is buried deep within the theme, and the working-out of the score is all about bringing round the theme’s restatement in that key, at the very end. Ballade No. 3 in A-flat, Op. 47 (1841) is nearly monothematic, its central, songlike melody interlaced with countermelodies throughout. Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52 (1842–43), illustrates the harmonic scheme of delaying the dominant chord—the chord that defines the key—until the moment of climax. In this case, the dominant is voiced in a hushed pianissimo right before the steely blast of octaves and chromatic runs th at ring d own the curtain. https://www.techtimes.com/articles/32456.text: On the evening of August 9, 2026, a 0.7-meter (27.6-inch) reflector at Kyiv's Observational Station Lisnyky held its gaze on a faint binary star designated Gaia24aeg for just over three hours — and in that single observing run, captured periodic pulses of extra light that place the object in one of the rarest and most theoretically important corners of stellar astrophysics. The find was reported in ATel #17962, published August 12, and demonstrates how a global distributed-telescope alerting pipeline is accelerating the pace of rare stellar classification.Gaia24aeg, also cataloged as AT 2024re and ASASSN-18hr, belongs to the ER Ursae Majoris (ER UMa) class of dwarf novae — a small group of binary star systems in which a white dwarf feeds so rapidly from a companion star's mass overflow that the system erupts into superoutburst roughly once every eight weeks, far more often than any ordinary dwarf nova. The detection of characteristic periodic brightness oscillations called superhumps during the current superoutburst, reported in ATel #17962 by a team from the Astronomical Scientific Point of the Department of Physics at Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv together with collaborators from the University of Wrocław and the University of Warsaw, is consistent with the system's Gaia Science Alerts ER UMa entry and provides real-time photometric evidence during an active eruption — exactly the kind of live data that allows researchers to characterize the object's binary parameters and refine its disk physics.How the Alert System Found the OutburstThe detection did not begin at a telescope. It began with software. The team had enrolled Gaia24aeg in BHTOM's coordination platform (Black Hole Target and Observation Manager), a European Union-funded coordination hub for time-domain astronomy built on the open-source TOM Toolkit developed by Las Cumbres Observatory. BHTOM's Outbursts Alerting System watched the target's running light curve — assembled automatically from data uploaded by contributing telescopes around the world — and flagged when a new brightening appeared at a timing consistent with the next expected superoutburst window, as detailed in ATel #17962's alert methods.BHTOM currently pools data from more than 130 telescopes worldwide, ranging from 0.2-meter (7.9-inch) amateur instruments to 2.5-meter (8.2-foot) professional facilities across multiple continents. The platform automatically performs PSF photometry on uploaded images, standardizes the output to Gaia Synthetic Photometry, and combines processed observations with archival survey data to produce calibrated light curves in near real time. Its funding comes from the European Union's Horizon 2020 OPTICON-RadioNet Pilot programme (grant 101004719, 2021–2025) and the Horizon Europe ACME programme (grant 101131928, 2024–2028).When the alert fired, lead author D. Yu. Rusanova and colleagues pointed the 0.7-m (27.6-in) AZT-8 Ritchey-Chrétien reflector at Lisnyky toward Gaia24aeg and began time-resolved photometry — rapid, continuous imaging designed to capture the short-period brightness oscillations that identify a superoutburst rather than an ordinary outburst. The ATel #17962 observation log records the session from MJD 61261.83 to MJD 61261.97635 (corresponding to approximately 15:55 ET to 19:25 ET on August 9, 2026), covering a span of roughly 3.4 hours.What Are Superhumps, and Why Do They Betray a Superoutburst?A dwarf nova is a binary system in which a white dwarf and a companion star orbit each other closely enough that gravity pulls material from the companion through a stream that spirals into a disk around the white dwarf. In quiescence the disk slowly accumulates material; periodically, when the disk temperature reaches the hydrogen ionization threshold, a thermal instability tips the disk into a hot, ionized, high-viscosity state — a normal outburst. In the rarer, brighter superoutburst, the disk swells to a critical radius: the point where disk material orbiting at three times the companion's period falls into 3:1 gravitational resonance with the companion's orbital motion.At 3:1 resonance, the companion's tidal pull repeatedly tugs on the same region of the disk at the same orbital phase, deforming the disk from a nearly circular ring into an elongated, eccentric shape. That eccentric disk then slowly precesses — rotating its long axis forward — and as different amounts of disk material pass through the changing gravitational landscape, the heating and viscous dissipation oscillate. The result is a repeating pulse of extra brightness riding a few percent above the underlying outburst light curve, with a period slightly longer than the binary's orbital period. That pulse is the positive superhump, and its presence is the thermal-tidal instability signature that distinguishes a superoutburst from an ordinary outburst, which shows no superhumps.In the Lisnyky light curve, the superhumps were unambiguous. The team detected a superhump period per ATel #17962 of 0.077 ± 0.003 days (approximately 111 minutes) with a peak-to-peak amplitude of roughly 0.15 magnitudes, determined using a Lomb-Scargle periodogram implemented in scipy.signal.lombscargle. The Lomb-Scargle method detects periodicity in unevenly spaced time series — the standard situation in ground-based astronomy, where gaps from Earth's rotation, weather, and telescope scheduling can break up a continuous observing run. Applied to three and a half hours of photometry, it cleanly resolved the superhump cycle against the underlying brightness envelope.Rare Company: What ER UMa Stars AreNot all superoutbursting binaries recur this frequently. SU Ursae Majoris-type dwarf novae — the broad class of short-orbital-period systems that undergo both normal outbursts and superoutbursts — typically cycle between superoutbursts over periods of several months to years. The ER UMa-type stars are the extreme end of that spectrum. Named after the prototype ER Ursae Majoris, classified as SU UMa subtype in 1995 by Taichi Kato and Chatief Kunjaya, these objects undergo superoutbursts roughly every 19 to 65 days.The theoretical explanation for such compressed behavior is a mass-transfer rate from the companion elevated enough to keep the accretion disk near the thermal instability threshold almost continuously. The disk is fed so rapidly that it needs only a small additional push to tip over into superoutburst. Because it rarely cools fully between events, normal outbursts — the shorter, dimmer cousins of superoutbursts — have almost no room between superoutburst cycles. The most extreme known ER UMa exemplar, RZ Leonis Minoris, originally held a supercycle of just 19 days, so close to permanent thermal stability that Kato 2016 documented novalike transition toward a permanently bright state.Five objects made up the canonical ER UMa census when it was first formally assembled in the early 2000s: ER UMa itself, RZ LMi, DI UMa, V1159 Ori, and IX Dra, all with supercycles between 18.9 and 54 days. Since the Zwicky Transient Facility began full-sky operations, subsequent surveys have substantially expanded that roster: Kato and Kojiguchi (2021) identified MGAB-V859 and ZTF18abgjsdg as ER UMa-type systems with supercycles of approximately 55 days and 58 days respectively, and a 2023 study by Kato documented CM Mic and related standstill systems — including DDE 48, MGAB-V728, and several others — showing ER UMa behavior with occasional standstills.Gaia24aeg's supercycle of 55 to 65 days places it at the longer end of the confirmed ER UMa range, alongside those ZTF-discovered members. The detection of superhumps during the current event is consistent with its established ER UMa designation and supplies real-time photometric evidence of the thermal-tidal mechanism in action.Why Astronomers Care About a Census Still in ProgressER UMa-type systems serve as extreme test cases for the disk instability model (DIM), the theoretical framework that explains dwarf nova outbursts as thermal-viscous cycles between cool, neutral disk states and hot, ionized ones. The DIM makes specific predictions about how the ratio of mass-transfer rate to the critical stability threshold governs supercycle length — predictions that ER UMa stars stress-test more severely than any other CV subtype, because they operate right at the edge between recurrent outbursting and permanent thermal stability. The Dubus 2018 DIM testing study confirms this framework's quantitative predictions against a sample of cataclysmic variables.There is a broader astrophysical application as well. The thermal-viscous disk instability physics in dwarf novae are formally analogous to those operating in X-ray binaries — compact systems where the accreting object is a neutron star or black hole rather than a white dwarf. Studying the full parameter space of disk instabilities, including the ER UMa extreme, helps theorists calibrate unified accretion disk models in systems that are nearby, bright, and observable in ordinary optical light, without requiring space-based X-ray telescopes.The catch is statistical: a population of perhaps 10 to 20 confirmed members is not large enough to test the DIM's quantitative predictions with robust statistical power. Each new confirmed ER UMa-type system, caught through real-time superhump detection rather than retrospective archival analysis, adds a data point that the population-level tests genuinely need. Tracking how Gaia24aeg's superhump period evolves through all three recognized stages — A, B, and C, corresponding to the disk's eccentric growth, steady precession, and decline — will allow a refined estimate of the binary mass ratio, while monitoring sharpens Gaia24aeg's supercycle measurement itself.How Does the Gaia-to-BHTOM-to-ATel Pipeline Work?The Gaia24aeg result illustrates what time-domain astronomy looks like when the infrastructure is working as designed. The European Space Agency's Gaia satellite first flagged the object in January 2024 — it appeared as a 2-magnitude candidate CV brightening and was labeled a candidate cataclysmic variable — but its precise subtype remained unclassified. The object accumulated a history of observed outbursts in the ASAS-SN and Gaia survey databases; at some earlier point, the team established its ER UMa designation based on the observed supercycle of 55 to 65 days. What August 2026 added was superhump detection during a live eruption — the first such confirmation of the TTI mechanism in this specific object.That progression from survey alert to BHTOM enrollment to automated superoutburst alert to targeted photometry to published ATel circular happened in a matter of days. A single 3.4-hour observing run with a 0.7-meter (27.6-inch) instrument produced data sufficient to settle the classification and provide the binary parameter inputs that more detailed modeling will need. The authors have now invited the broader astronomical community to upload observations to BHTOM for Gaia24aeg (bhtom.space/public/targets/Gaia24aeg), where all submitted data are automatically processed and added to the cumulative light curve — opening the follow-up campaign to any telescope capable of imaging a 16th-to-18th-magnitude target.The Rusanova team published three related ATel circulars in a three-week span around this result — ATel #17932 on Gaia20eud, ATel #17951 on Gaia20ffw, and now ATel #17962 on Gaia24aeg — suggesting a systematic BHTOM-enabled classification program running across multiple Gaia-alerted candidate CVs simultaneously. Each new confirmed superhump detection narrows the gap between the ER UMa population the theoretical models require and the population the observational record can actually deliver.Frequently Asked QuestionsWhat is a dwarf nova and how is it different from a regular nova?A dwarf nova is a binary star system in which a white dwarf accretes material from a companion through an accretion disk. When the disk reaches a critical temperature, a thermal instability causes it to transition from a cool, dim state to a hot, bright one — producing an outburst that can repeat every few days to decades. A classical nova is physically different: hydrogen fuses explosively on the white dwarf's surface in a runaway thermonuclear reaction, producing a far brighter and less predictable event. Dwarf novae are powered entirely by disk physics, not surface fusion.What are superhumps in a binary star system, and why do they identify a superoutburst?Superhumps are periodic brightness pulses that appear on top of a superoutburst's underlying light curve, with a period slightly longer than the binary's orbital period. They arise when the accretion disk swells to a radius where orbiting material falls into 3:1 gravitational resonance with the companion star — causing the disk to become eccentric and precess. Each orbit of the eccentric disk past the companion produces a tidal heating pulse. Their presence proves the thermal-tidal instability mechanism is driving the event and distinguishes a superoutburst from an ordinary outburst, which shows no superhumps.What makes ER UMa-type dwarf novae so extreme compared to other cataclysmic variables?ER UMa-type systems undergo superoutbursts every 19 to 65 days — far more frequently than the typical SU UMa-type dwarf nova, which might cycle between superoutbursts over months to years. The high recurrence rate reflects an unusually elevated mass-transfer rate from the companion, keeping the accretion disk perennially close to thermal instability and nearly eliminating the breathing room between eruption cycles. At the extreme end of the class, RZ Leonis Minoris (supercycle ~19 days) has been observed partially transitioning toward a permanently bright nova-like state — the point at which outbursts cease because the disk never cools at all. Gaia24aeg, with a supercycle of 55 to 65 days, sits at the longer end of this rare category.How does the BHTOM network enable real-time classification of rare stellar phenomena?BHTOM functions as a coordination hub between automated sky surveys — like Gaia — and the individual telescopes that follow up on alerts. Enrolled targets are monitored continuously by data uploaded from more than 130 contributing telescopes worldwide; the platform's automated pipeline standardizes all incoming photometry. When a target's light curve shows brightening consistent with a predicted outburst window, an alert fires — enabling rapid targeted follow-up with a dedicated instrument before the event peaks or ends. The result, as in Gaia24aeg's case, is classification during an active eruption rather than weeks later through archival analysis. Anyone with a telescope capable of reaching 16th-magnitude targets can contribute observations directly to the Gaia24aeg BHTOM page and become part of the ongoing campaign.

Photograph: China Daily/Reuters Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Fifteen Britons among 261 foreigners missing in China after floods Total number of missing Britons between Tibet and Nepal at 48 as Beijing mobilises more than 2,100 rescue workers Raphael Boyd Sun 30 Aug 2026 13.13 EDT Last modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 16.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Fifteen British nationals are reported to be missing in China as the search continues for survivors of the devastating flooding in Nepal and Tibet. Nepali and Chinese authorities confirmed an updated death toll of at least 810 on Sunday. More than 3,000 people are believed missing after flash floods triggered by a massive glacier collapse in the Himalayas on Wednesday engulfed Gyirong port on the Nepal-China border. ‘The river has taken everything’: people return to remains of their homes in Nepal Read more The 15 missing British people are among 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries missing in China, according to figures released by Chinese authorities, bringing the total of missing Britons between Tibet and Nepal to 48. The Tibet autonomous region’s government said the total missing there also included 104 Nepalis, 49 people from India, 33 from Latvia and 18 from the US. Thirty-three British people had already been declared missing on the Nepal side of the border. Some were on a pilgrimage at the time of the flood, including Hemangini Jitendra Patel and Hema Sunil Amin , two sisters who were last seen on the Friendship Bridge on the border. The figure for missing Americans has been disputed by the US state department, which declared on Sunday that at least 85 US citizens were missing. The department’s spokesperson, Tommy Pigott, said getting accurate information from the region had been difficult, “made even more so by the devastation and the remoteness that we see”. Chinese authorities have said at least 16 people have died on their side of the border. But there are concerns over a possible lack of transparency from the Chinese government, which has prevented footage of the floods from being shared in the country and may have downplayed the casualties. Police in Nepal said 794 people had been confirmed to have died there and at least 2,742 injured. Numerous areas remain at risk of fresh flooding and people who have returned to their homes have been told to remain alert and be prepared to evacuate again at short notice. View image in fullscreen Army personnel conduct a search and rescue operation for flood victims along the Narayani River in Nepal’s Chitwan district on Sunday. Photograph: Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty Images Rescue efforts have been affected by the threat of landslides and dangerous weather as well as confusion over which side of the border victims had been on when the waters struck. Chinese state television reported that officials in Beijing, far better resourced than their Nepali counterparts, had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated more than 220m yuan (£24m) to support relief efforts. Equipment and supplies have been airdropped to frontline workers, while Chinese soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing, CCTV said. The Chinese premier, Li Qiang, had already travelled to the region. Numerous countries have pledged to help Nepal, including the US, which has offered $3.6m (£2.7m) in humanitarian aid, “including up to three months of emergency food assistance to up to 10,000 flood-affected households”, on top of $500,000 previously pledged, and Australia, which will donate more than $3m in assistance. Britain has committed £5m to Nepal and sent a rapid deployment team, which arrived in Kathmandu on Saturday. A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: “We are working around the clock to support British nationals and their families affected by the devastating floods on the Nepal-China border. We are coordinating closely with the Nepali and Chinese authorities and have deployed consular support staff to the region to ensure British nationals can access support.” Explore more on these topics Nepal-Tibet flood disaster Tibet China Nepal South and central Asia news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Headteacher saves 900 children from deadly flash flood in Nepal ‘The river has taken everything’: people return to remains of their homes in Nepal Nepal-Tibet deaths from flash flooding rise amid race to free workers in tunnel Number of missing in Nepal and Tibet rises to 3,000 as bad weather hampers search Daughter traces mother and aunt’s last known location in Nepal through TikTok video ‘Their whole village has disappeared’: frantic hunt for survivors in Kathmandu hospital What we know about the Australians missing in the Nepal floods At least 90 Americans missing in Nepal flood among 2,000 unaccounted for ‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal At least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floods, says Red Cross Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/31/six-w.text: A car bomb exploded in front of a police station in Mexico on Sunday night, wounding six people, authorities said.The blast happened in the town of Ojocaliente in Zacatecas, a state with key routes for drug trafficking."The explosive was placed in a private vehicle and caused physical damage to the station and properties located nearby," state government secretary Rodrigo Reyes said in a post on Facebook."Six civilians have been reported wounded, who are receiving medical care," he said in an earlier post.Zacatecas is key to the drug trade because it links central Mexico with the north and west of the country and features routes that are key to smuggling cocaine and other narcotics to the United States.Horrific drug violence plagued the state for years, with bodies turning up and people going missing almost on a daily basis until relative calm set in.But in July, five bodies appeared hanging from a bridge in the town of Pozos de Gamboa, about 75 kilometres from Ojocaliente.The victims included a former mayor, civil servants and business people from other parts of the state.

Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The Guardian View image in fullscreen A drone operator brings one into land on Coogee beach. Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The Guardian Sharks Sydney’s beaches enter the drone age to get swimmers back in the water after spate of shark attacks Seventy beaches across New South Wales are part of the $34m dawn-to-dusk drone-monitoring program, which one expert has called ‘the best technology we have at the moment’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Penry Buckley Tue 1 Sep 2026 12.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 16.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “Hey Taha, what’s the visibility like?” shouts a man with a towel slung over his shoulder. “Uh, nice,” says Surf Life Saving New South Wales drone operator Taha Kafil-Hussain. “Good?” the man asks. “Very good,” Kafil-Hussain assures him. Thanking him, the early morning swimmer turns and heads down the steps to Coogee beach. Kafil-Hussain, who Guardian Australia has joined on his early morning shark surveillance flight, says: “When they’re local, they just want to see what the weather, what the water looks like, [if there’s] anything scary.” The 22-year-old has been flying drones for SLS NSW for four years, but only at Coogee beach for a matter of weeks. Before a shark attack on 34-year-old Sydney teacher and mother Leah Stewart in June, drone surveillance was not permitted at Coogee because it lies directly under the flight path from Sydney airport’s east-west runway. In an interview with 60 Minutes broadcast on Sunday, Stewart described the horror encounter with a four-metre white shark, after which her left arm was amputated, as “like fighting a dinosaur” . The attack, one of a series of high-profile incidents in Sydney in the past 12 months, has prompted the state government to massively ramp up its shark mitigation program. View image in fullscreen During each drone flight, Taha Kafil-Hussain rakes the bay in sections from left to right, backwards and forwards, leaving a checkerboard pattern on his control screen Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Kafil-Hussain has now flown drones at most Sydney beaches, from Palm Beach in the north to Cronulla in the south. Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The Guardian Under a $34m initiative by the state government which rolled out on 1 July, 38 of Sydney’s ocean beaches, including Coogee, now receive dawn-to-dusk drone monitoring year round. Seventy NSW beaches in total are part of the dawn-to-dusk program, while others will benefit from increased surveillance throughout the summer and school holidays. On Tuesday, surveillance hours will increase, running from 6.15am to 5pm each day for the start of spring, as daylight increases. When Guardian Australia meets Kafil-Hussain in mid-winter, he arrives at 6.30am to throw up a marquee, before checking a radio to determine which direction the planes are flying in (drone surveillance at Coogee has been allowed with special permission from the airport). Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Not long after, the drone takes off in a whir of plastic from a miniature landing pad, rising 60 metres into the air before heading out to sea. During each 20-minute flight, Kafil-Hussain rakes the bay in sections from left to right, backwards and forwards, leaving a checkerboard pattern on his control screen. He says he’s looking for “anything moving in a different way than normal”. “Anything moving against the flow of water, anything that looks a little bit long – anything alive, really.” He pauses when he thinks he’s spotted something, to zoom in. “Looks like seaweed,” he says. University of Sydney shark policy expert and associate professor Christopher Pepin-Neff agrees that “drones are the best technology that we have at the moment”. But they say there are “important caveats that we need to give to the public”. “On days that are windy, if the shark is too small, the drone operator is not going to be able to see a shark if it’s there. “I’m slightly nervous that, in the absence of [a] large public education campaign, we have the possibility that we’re going to scare the shit out of people,” says Pepin-Neff. With more drone surveillance comes more regular shark sightings. The NSW government says there have been more 750 sightings and more than 200 intervention actions by Surf Life Saving NSW since 1 July. Shark listening stations are now tracking 1,698 white sharks, 938 tiger sharks and 374 bull sharks – the “target sharks” which are most frequently involved in serious shark bites. Kafil-Hussain says he has seen more bull and tiger sharks than whites, and has raised the alarm a few times, most recently for a bronze whaler – involved in rare attacks – which he initially thought was a target shark. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion If it’s early and he’s on his own, raising the alarm means making the call to clear the water himself – otherwise he shares what he has seen with lifeguards and they make the decision, with the time from spotting a hazard to fully clearing the water about two or three minutes. The SLS drones have a speaker attached to them, allowing him to communicate directly with surfers and swimmers. It’s a technology familiar to followers of the Instagram account Drone Shark App, run by Jason Iggleden, who has been using a drone since 2018 to surveil beaches including Bondi, Tamarama and Bronte. View image in fullscreen Christopher Pepin-Neff says the drone program will ‘restore confidence’ ahead of a busy summer, but there is ‘no silver bullet’. Photograph: Steven Markham/AFP/Getty Images Videos on the account show an enormous seal barrel-rolling through the water and a swirling vortex of Australian salmon, while in another a whale lingers beneath a kayaker in Tamarama. “I just had a bit of a vision to help … with getting people out of water with sharks, and just showing them the beauty of what’s out there,” he said. The licensed and insured drone flyer, who continues to work independently, now passes on any sightings to SLS NSW. He is a firm believer in the drone surveillance, saying the ability to spot target sharks grows with experience. “I don’t think you really need to consider much more than drones, to be honest,” he says. Pepin-Neff is supportive of other non-lethal technologies, such as SMART drum lines. They say a trial of new artificial intelligence detection software on drones will take the pressure off humans to discern between more and less dangerous sharks. But their message on controversial measures like shark nets, here to stay on NSW beaches, and culling, is unequivocal: “They do not work.” ‘Not a perfect solution’ Kafil-Hussain, who drives each day from his home in Parramatta, has now flown drones at most Sydney beaches, from Palm Beach in the north to Cronulla in the south. Every beach is different – he sees turtles, dolphins, the occasional whale. Coogee is home to a wobbegong, a low-swimming carpet shark which does not hunt humans but can attack if threatened. “He’s not around. He’ll pop out eventually,” says Kafil-Hussain. When Guardian Australia visits the beach, arriving before sunrise, it is already heaving with eastern suburbs dog walkers, swim clubs and surfers. Just weeks after the attack on Stewart, Kafil-Hussain says numbers at the beach have only been growing. Pepin-Neff says the drone program will “restore confidence” ahead of a busy summer, but there is “no silver bullet”. “Drones are a great tool but they’re not a perfect solution.” Pepin-Neff swims at fully enclosed beaches, like Marrinawi Cove in Barangaroo, but their advice for those that swim at unenclosed beaches: “Swim between the flags.” “The ocean is the wild and we need to treat the beach like the bush.” Explore more on these topics Sharks New South Wales Sydney Marine life news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution

https://www.cnb.cz/en/cnb-news/press-rel.text: Home News archive Press releases Press releases 21. 9. 2026 Banknotes and coins Anniversary CZK 5,000 banknote enters circulation; exchange at CNB offices starts on Tuesday Share The Czech National Bank (CNB) will issue a 2023 version CZK 5,000 banknote with a special additional print tomorrow, Tuesday 22 September 2026. The issue commemorates the 100th anniversary of the commencement of operations of the National Bank of Czechoslovakia, the first independent central bank of Czechoslovakia. A total of 200,000 banknotes with the additional print have been produced. The banknotes will be available only in exchange for Czech banknotes of the corresponding value at the cash offices of the CNB’s branches in Prague, Brno, Hradec Králové and Ostrava. The exchange is limited to a maximum of three anniversary banknotes per person. The exchange will start on Tuesday 22 September 2026 and continue while stocks last. The CNB’s cash offices will be open on working days from 7.30 a.m. to 4 p.m.* * From Tuesday 29 September 2026, the opening hours of the CNB's cash offices change. They are open on working days from 7.30 a.m. to 11.30 a.m. and from 12.30 p.m. to 2 p.m. Access to the cash offices at all CNB branches will be via the main entrances to the CNB buildings. Information boards and leaflets have been prepared for members of the public. The CNB has also published an instructional video demonstrating the exchange procedure. The video is available on the CNB’s website and its YouTube channel (in Czech only). “By issuing this anniversary banknote, we are commemorating 100 years since the commencement of operations of the National Bank of Czechoslovakia, which laid the foundations of modern central banking in our country. I believe it will appeal not only to collectors, but also to people interested in the history of our currency and Czech banking,” says CNB Bank Board member Karina Kubelková. The anniversary banknote has the same dimensions, design and other parameters as the standard 2023 version CZK 5,000 banknote in circulation and is legal tender in the Czech Republic. It differs from the standard banknote in having a special additional print consisting of foil with nano effects hot-stamped on the banknote. The foil has a silver metallic design with variable colour effects that change depending on the viewing angle and the angle of incident light. The main motif of the nanostructure is the CNB’s special logo marking the 100th anniversary of the commencement of operations of the National Bank of Czechoslovakia, designed by graphic designer Jan Solpera, who also designed the lettering on Czech banknotes. The additional print also features two portraits of the first President of Czechoslovakia, Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, and a QR code linking to the CNB’s webpages dedicated to the anniversary. Members of the public will also be able to purchase a unique presentation sleeve designed to hold the anniversary banknote. A total of 30,000 sleeves have been produced. The sleeve, priced at CZK 100 including VAT, will be available at the same cash offices, with purchases limited to one per person. Payment can be made in cash, by payment card or by instant payment via a QR code. The exchange of the anniversary banknotes will follow the same procedure as a standard cash transaction at a CNB cash office. Cash office staff will verify the authenticity and validity of the banknotes presented and then issue the corresponding number of anniversary banknotes with the additional print. Key information on the anniversary banknote and presentation sleeve Banknote face value: CZK 5,000 Version: 2023 with an additional print Issue date: 22 September 2026 Print run: 200,000 Exchange limit: maximum of three banknotes per person Method of payment: exchange only for Czech banknotes of the corresponding value Number of presentation sleeves: 30,000 Price of presentation sleeve: CZK 100 including VAT Purchase limit: one per person Method of payment: cash, payment card or instant payment via a QR code Distribution: exclusively through the CNB’s cash offices (Prague, Brno, Hradec Králové and Ostrava) Anniversary: 100 years since the commencement of operations of the National Bank of Czechoslovakia, the CNB’s predecessor Jaroslav Krejčí CNB Spokesperson Related links Photogallery Updated: 25 September 2026 News Press releases Calendar

https://www.sdjewishworld.com/2026/10/17.text: By Jerry Klinger in Boynton Beach, Florida Jerry Klinger Raoul Wallenberg Memory is an opportunity, a duty, an obligation. It can be denied only by deliberate erasure. Around the world and shockingly in the U.S., the denial of Holocaust memory is cancerously metastasizing. Because of the Jewish American Society for Historic Preservation, Holocaust Memory, and humanitarian courage beyond common understanding was not permitted to be erased. JASHP provided the funding and technical expertise without question or hesitation. Comments by the Raoul Wallenberg Association, Hungary about the dedication: A Tribute to the “Hero Without a Grave” Wallenberg plaque in Budapest, Hungary On October 15, 2026, the memorial plaque honoring Raoul Wallenberg was rededicated in a formal ceremony at the main entrance of the House of Fates (Sorsok Háza), located at the former Józsefváros railway station. The original plaque had been unveiled on January 17, 2006, but was stolen by unknown persons in 2013. Now, through the collaborative efforts of many, a fitting memorial once again marks the site where human destinies were decided in 1944. The text of the new plaque reads: “In late 1944, the Nazis’ Hungarian accomplices dispatched thousands of the remaining Jews from this station to the death camps. In November and December of 1944, Swedish diplomat Raoul Wallenberg saved hundreds of Jews from the ‘death trains’ on three separate occasions through his courageous personal intervention, securing their release by means of Swedish documents.” The event was opened by Dr. József Sebes, President of the Raoul Wallenberg Association. Speeches were delivered by Karin Olofsdotter, Administrative State Secretary at the Swedish Ministry for Foreign Affairs and former Swedish Ambassador to Budapest; Diana Madunic, Sweden’s Ambassador to Budapest; and historian Prof. Dr. Szabolcs Szita. According to József Sebes, it was a truly extraordinary feat—almost beyond comprehension—that Raoul Wallenberg, through his courageous and heroic actions, saved hundreds of people from certain death at this railway station. In his speech, he also shared a personal story: Dr. Yvette Kardos—a recipient of the Wallenberg Prize and an association representative—shared that her own grandfather was saved at this very railway station. Following a suggestion from Wallenberg, he presented a laundry receipt he happened to have in his pocket as a letter of safe conduct—a document that was, miraculously, accepted. Subsequently, Karin Olofsdotter, Director General for Administrative Affairs at the Swedish Ministry for Foreign Affairs (and former Swedish Ambassador to Budapest), and Diana Madunic, the current Swedish Ambassador to Budapest, delivered speeches. Both paid tribute to the courage and example of Raoul Wallenberg, whose legacy continues to connect the Swedish and Hungarian peoples to this day. Prof. Szabolcs Szita, former director of the Holocaust Documentation Center, delivered an address titled “Painful Remembrance.” He recounted the long journey undertaken by those who have fought to preserve this memorial site. Various proposals were put forward to save the railway station and transform it into an authentic memorial—including a plan for a “House of Remembrance” dedicated to the Jewish children who were killed. However, the fate of the building complex remains uncertain, and the physical traces of the past at the site continue to be at risk. It is, therefore, of particular significance that Raoul Wallenberg’s memorial plaque has been restored today—along with the memory of the mass rescue operations so inextricably linked to his name. We extend our thanks to State Secretary Karin Olofsdotter and Ambassador Diana Madunic for today’s gesture and for their presence. We are grateful to Jane and Martin Sugarman (United Kingdom) and the Jewish American Society for Historic Preservation, whose support made the creation of the new plaque possible. We thank Prof. Szabolcs Szita for his moving and thought-provoking words, as well as everyone who joined us to commemorate together. Raoul Wallenberg has no grave. His memory is preserved by the places where he saved lives—and by us, who ensure that these places do not fade into oblivion. Raoul Wallenberg Association Budapest, October 15, 2026 * Jerry Klinger is the founder of the Jewish American Society for Historic Preservation.
